analysis.one_liner: Designates all PFAS 'forever chemicals' as hazardous substances and bans them in food packaging.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any floor action after being referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in January 2020.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the EPA to designate the entire class of PFAS chemicals — man-made 'forever chemicals' used in nonstick cookware, water-repellent clothing, and firefighting foam — as hazardous substances, making polluters liable for cleanup. It would also add PFAS to the list of hazardous air pollutants, ban PFAS in food packaging starting January 2022, prohibit incinerating PFAS firefighting foam and other PFAS waste, and fund water filtration for contaminated household wells and grants for affected water systems. The bill was introduced by Sen. Sanders with two Democratic cosponsors and never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 100 million Americans the bill's findings say may be drinking PFAS-contaminated water, owners of contaminated household wells (who would get grants for filtration systems), and communities near military bases and industrial sites with PFAS pollution. The bill's own findings state PFAS were found in the blood of 99 percent of Americans and that the EPA was first notified of the health risks in 1998 but never set a drinking water standard [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to designate all PFAS as hazardous substances under the Superfund law (CERCLA) within one year, which makes parties responsible for releases liable for cleanup costs.
Bans PFAS in food contact substances — materials that touch food during manufacturing, packing, or holding — effective January 1, 2022, by deeming any such use unsafe.
Adds all PFAS to the Clean Air Act list of hazardous air pollutants within 180 days and requires EPA to identify major and area sources of PFAS air emissions.

Prohibits disposing of PFAS-containing firefighting foam and other PFAS waste by incineration, which the bill treats as spreading contamination into the air, and makes PFAS waste a hazardous waste for criminal penalty purposes.

Authorizes grants so owners of contaminated household water wells can buy and install filtration systems, plus grant programs for affected community water systems and for publicly owned treatment works to meet new PFAS pretreatment standards.

Requires the Department of Defense to report on its stockpiled PFAS-containing firefighting foam and how it has been destroyed; the bill's findings note DoD estimates military-base PFAS cleanup will exceed its original $2 billion estimate.

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers and industrial users, who would face Superfund cleanup liability once the chemicals are designated hazardous; food packaging and food-contact material makers, who would have to reformulate by 2022; water utilities and treatment works facing new pretreatment standards; and taxpayers, who would fund the open-ended grant programs and share the cost of the Defense Department's cleanup, which the bill's findings say will exceed $2 billion.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS makers, packaging firms, utilities, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill regulates PFAS as a single class of 'all PFAS' — thousands of man-made chemicals with at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom — rather than chemical by chemical, so substances with different risk profiles would all face the same hazardous-substance designation, air-pollutant listing, and liability, raising compliance costs across many industries.
The grant programs for water filtration, treatment works, and infrastructure are authorized at 'such sums as are necessary,' leaving the federal cost open-ended rather than capped.

Designating PFAS as hazardous substances under CERCLA creates cleanup liability that would fall on water utilities, landfills, and other passive receivers of PFAS as well as manufacturers, and the bill's own findings put Defense Department cleanup costs above $2 billion, a cost ultimately borne by taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong: the bill's findings describe contamination in more than 1,400 communities, an estimated 100 million people potentially drinking contaminated water, an EPA health advisory of 70 parts per trillion that a 2018 federal health agency study found too permissive, and $13.7 billion in estimated costs from PFAS-linked low-birth-weight births. The bill pairs its mandates with money — filtration grants, treatment-works grants, and infrastructure funding — which blunts cost complaints from water systems. The main honest objections are that regulating all PFAS as one class is a blunt instrument and that the spending authority is uncapped.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 28, 2020, read twice, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat with no further action of any kind through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on January 28, 2020, joined by Sens. Merkley and Markey.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction; that referral is the last action in the bill's history.

The bill's findings state PFAS have been found in the blood of 99 percent of people in the United States, are confirmed in groundwater or tap water of more than 1,400 communities, and may contaminate drinking water for more than 100 million people.

The findings also state the EPA was first notified of PFAS health risks in 1998 but had failed to set a drinking water standard or restrict ongoing releases, and that the Defense Department estimates PFAS cleanup on military bases will surpass its original $2 billion estimate.
No vote was ever held in the committee or on the Senate floor, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died without consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and industrial users avoided the Superfund cleanup liability, food-packaging firms avoided the 2022 reformulation mandate, and no one had to fund the water filtration and treatment grants — at the cost of leaving the contamination the bill described unaddressed at the federal level.

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 28, 2020, designating all PFAS as hazardous substances, banning PFAS in food packaging, and funding filtration and cleanup programs.

against.name: John Bhojani seatholder, Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or committee vote; the bill's action history ends with its referral to the committee.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; the bill never left committee in the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Sanders and two Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist to test whether the split was strictly partisan.

industries.industry: PFAS chemical manufacturers and industrial users
industries.note: Designating all PFAS as hazardous substances under Superfund would make these companies liable for cleanup of the contamination the bill's findings say has spread to more than 1,400 communities. Their cost of cleaning up is the public's gain, and the industry's interest ran against the bill.

industries.industry: Food packaging and food-contact material makers
industries.note: The bill deems any PFAS use in materials touching food unsafe beginning January 1, 2022, forcing reformulation or product withdrawal. States like Washington and Maine had already begun restricting PFAS food packaging, per the bill's findings.

industries.industry: Firefighting foam manufacturers and waste incinerators
industries.note: The bill bans incinerating PFAS-containing firefighting foam and other PFAS wastes, cutting off a disposal channel and requiring the Defense Department to account for its stockpiled foam.

industries.industry: Water utilities and publicly owned treatment works
industries.note: They would face new PFAS pretreatment standards and possible cleanup liability, but the bill funds grants to help them comply and to protect affected community water systems.

The bill requires a report on the Pentagon's PFAS foam stockpile and destruction methods; its findings note DoD already expects cleanup costs above $2 billion on military bases, a burden shared by taxpayers.
